goals.title: Be able to write and understand very basic Python scripts
goals.description: You can write and understand short Python scripts that use `print()`, variables, and basic mathematical operators. You understand how these building blocks interact to produce simple outputs.

children.title: Use print() correctly
children.description: You can display text or numbers on screen with the print() function and understand when to use quotes around text versus numbers.
suggestions: Begin with examples and let students predict what each line will print.
Ask them to explain why certain lines cause errors (e.g. missing quotes).
Follow up with short tasks where they must write the `print()` statements themselves.
When you ask to explain print methods, limit to 4 at a time.
Do not use sep or len
Be creative in the worlds you print. Don't use typical phrasing like 'Hello World'

children.title: Work with variables
children.description: You can create and use variables to store values, and you understand the difference between text (`str`), integers (`int`), and real numbers (`float`).
suggestions: Use simple examples to show how variable values can change during execution.
Contrast code that uses `"5"` (a string) and `5` (a number) and discuss what happens.
Provide small exercises where students must fix or complete snippets with incorrect variable usage.

children.title: Apply basic mathematical operators
children.description: You can use Python’s basic mathematical operators (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `**`, `//`, `%`) and understand how they behave with different types of numbers.
suggestions: Start with `+`, `-`, `*`, and `/`, then introduce `**`, `//`, and `%` once the basics are secure.
Let students predict the result before running each expression.
Include examples that mix integers and floats, and demonstrate what happens when math operators are used with strings.

goals.title: Be able to write and understand conditional statements
goals.description: You can write and understand Python programs that make decisions using `if`, `elif`, and `else` statements. You know how comparison and logical operators control program flow.

children.title: Understand comparison operators
children.description: You can compare values using operators such as `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, and `>=`, and predict whether an expression is `True` or `False`.
suggestions: Present short examples and have students state which lines evaluate to `True`.
Use real-life contexts (“Is temperature > 30?”) to make the logic meaningful.
Follow up with small prediction tasks before moving to coding exercises.

children.title: Use `if` and `else` statements
children.description: You can write simple conditional statements that execute different code depending on whether a condition is true or false.
suggestions: Let students convert such sentences into code step by step.
Gradually increase complexity by nesting.
Start from natural-language examples.
do not require the use of elif yet.
Do not require the use of combined conditions.

children.title: Use `elif` and combine conditions logically
children.description: You can chain multiple conditions with `elif` and use logical operators (`and`, `or`, `not`) to combine them.
suggestions: Show how `elif` avoids redundant `if` statements.
Practice truth tables for `and` / `or` / `not` to clarify outcomes.
Design mini-projects like a grade classifier (“If score >= 90: … elif score >= 80: … else: …”).

goals.title: Be able to write and understand for-loops
goals.description: You can write and understand Python programs that use for loops to repeat actions. You know how iteration works over sequences such as lists, strings, and ranges.

children.title: Understand the structure of a for-loop
children.description: You can recognize and explain the syntax of a for loop and describe how it repeats actions for each item in a sequence.
suggestions: Start from natural-language examples.
Show loop headers and bodies separately to clarify indentation.

children.title: Use range() to control repetition
children.description: You can use range() to create sequences of numbers and control how many times a loop runs.
suggestions: Practice small examples like for i in range(5):.
Discuss start, stop, and step values.
Have students predict the output before running the code.
Use visual number lines to represent iteration.

children.title: Iterate over strings
children.description: You can loop through characters in a string, and access each element during the loop.
suggestions: Use concrete examples such as looping over a small sentence.
Show the difference between for x in string and for i in range(len(string)).
Play with vowels and consonants.

children.title: Combine loops with conditions
children.description: You can use if statements inside for loops to make decisions during iteration.
suggestions: Show filtering tasks (“print only even numbers”).
Let students write small data-processing scripts that mix repetition and selection.
Encourage reasoning about loop flow: when does the condition trigger?

goals.title: Be able to write and understand while-loops
goals.description: You can write and understand Python programs that use while loops to repeat actions until a condition is no longer true. You can decide when to use a while loop instead of a for loop.

children.title: Understand the structure of a while-loop
children.description: You can explain how a while loop checks a condition before each repetition, and how it stops when the condition becomes false.
suggestions: Compare the while loop to natural language
Let students predict how many times a simple while loop runs.
Show the importance of changing a variable inside the loop to avoid infinite repetition.
Use examples like counting up or down with a variable.

children.title: Use conditions and counters in while-loops
children.description: You can control a while loop using numeric counters and conditions.
suggestions: Ask students to describe in words what each part of the loop does.
Use interactive predictions (“what happens if we forget to update i?”).
Practice both increasing and decreasing counters.
Don't lead students in to executing infinite loops!

children.title: Choose between for and while
children.description: You can decide which type of loop fits a problem: use for when the number of repetitions is known, and while when it depends on a condition.
suggestions: Compare both loop types for similar tasks (“count from 1 to 5” vs. “keep counting until reached 5”).
Discuss readability and clarity as criteria for choosing.
Provide short mixed exercises where students must decide which loop is better suited.

children.title: Use break and continue to control loop flow
children.description: You can interrupt or skip parts of a loop using break and continue
suggestions: Show examples where break stops the loop early (e.g. stop at a certain number).
Show how continue skips the rest of one iteration but keeps looping.
Discuss typical mistakes like unreachable code after break.
Use simple counting examples to illustrate both commands clearly.

goals.title: Be able to create and work with lists
goals.description: You can create, access, and modify lists in Python. You understand that a list is an ordered collection of items that can be changed and iterated over.

children.title: Understand what a list is
children.description: You can explain what a list represents and recognize the syntax for creating one using square brackets.
suggestions: Show lists with different types of values (numbers, text, or mixed).
Compare a single variable with a list containing several values.
Let students predict what happens when printing a list or its type.

children.title: Access and modify list elements
children.description: You can retrieve and change elements in a list using their index.
suggestions: Highlight that the first element has index 0.
Demonstrate reading and updating items step by step.
Have students write short snippets that change one or more items and observe the result.
Encourage reasoning about what happens when indices go out of range.

children.title: Use len() and append()
children.description: You can measure the length of a list and add new elements to it dynamically.
suggestions: Show how the length changes after appending.
Combine both functions in short, progressive examples.
Encourage exploration of order: newly added items appear at the end.

children.title: Iterate over lists with for-loops
children.description: You can use a for loop to process each element in a list.
suggestions: Demonstrate both looping directly over elements and looping by index.
Encourage predicting outputs before execution.
Let students modify the loop body to perform small transformations or print patterns.
Alternate between lists of numbers and lists of short words to maintain variety.

children.title: Combine lists with conditions
children.description: You can use if statements inside loops to check or select certain elements.
suggestions: Ask conceptual questions about which items meet a condition.
Have students print, count, or collect items that fit a rule.
Emphasize how conditions work the same way inside a loop as outside it.
Encourage creative variations instead of repeating one fixed example type.
